The jumps add up to less than the array's length
nums[0] is smaller than the array's length
quiz.why: Track `farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])`. A 0 only blocks you if nothing earlier can jump past it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Jump Game**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Jump Game**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1).

quiz.q: Since the input is already sorted, insertion takes…
options: One linear pass: before, overlapping (merge), after
A binary search for the spot, then an O(1) insert
Pushing every interval into a heap by start
quiz.why: That takes O(n) time. Binary search finds the spot, but merging and shifting are still O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Insert Interval**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Insert Interval**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n) for the output.

quiz.q: After sorting by start, an interval overlaps the last merged one when…
quiz.why: Touching endpoints count as overlapping here.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Merge Intervals**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n log n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Merge Intervals**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: Which interval should you keep when two overlap?
quiz.why: An earlier end leaves the most room for the rest.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Non-overlapping Intervals**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n log n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Non-overlapping Intervals**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1) beyond sorting.

quiz.q: What does the min-heap of end times represent?
options: The rooms in use, with the soonest-free room on top
The rooms in use, with the latest-free room on top
Start times of the meetings still waiting for a room
quiz.why: The heap's final size is the peak number of concurrent meetings.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Meeting Rooms II**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n log n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Meeting Rooms II**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: How do you rotate a matrix 90° clockwise in place?
options: Transpose, then reverse the order of the rows
Reverse each row, then reverse each column
quiz.why: Check it on a 2×2 example. The two middle options rotate counter-clockwise, and the last one rotates 180°.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Rotate Image**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n²).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Rotate Image**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1).

quiz.q: Why re-check `top <= bottom` before walking the bottom row?
options: A single remaining row would otherwise be visited twice
Without it, the corner cells would be skipped
top can run past the last index of the matrix
The loop would otherwise stop one row early
quiz.why: The same goes for `left <= right` with a single column.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Spiral Matrix**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(m · n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Spiral Matrix**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1) besides the output.

quiz.q: How does the O(1)-space version remember which rows and columns to zero?
options: It uses the first row and first column as marker storage
It zeroes each row at once and the columns afterwards
It scans the matrix twice without storing anything
It copies the matrix and reads the zeros from the copy
quiz.why: Track row 0 separately, because it doubles as a marker row.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Set Matrix Zeroes**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(m · n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Set Matrix Zeroes**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1).

quiz.q: In bitwise addition, `(a & b) << 1` is…
options: The bits where a and b differ
quiz.why: `a ^ b` adds without carrying; repeat until the carry is 0.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Sum of Two Integers**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(32).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Sum of Two Integers**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1).

quiz.q: When do you shrink the window from the left?
options: While it still contains all the required characters
Whenever it grows longer than t, to keep it short
Whenever a character in the window repeats
Only once `right` has reached the end of s
quiz.why: Keep shrinking while it is still valid, recording the best window as you go.

quiz.q: Why push `(val, i, node)` into the heap instead of `(val, node)`?
options: Ties on val would compare ListNodes, which raises TypeError
So nodes from the same list keep their original order
Because heapq orders tuples by their last item first
Because ListNodes can't be hashed without an index
quiz.why: The unique index i breaks ties before Python ever compares nodes.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Merge K Sorted Lists**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(N log k).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Merge K Sorted Lists**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(k).

quiz.q: What does the recursive helper return to its parent?
options: The best downward path from this node, using one branch
The best path through this node, using both branches
The best path anywhere inside this node's subtree
The sum of every value in this node's subtree
quiz.why: A path passing up through the parent can only continue down one side. The both-branches path is used to update the global best, not returned.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(h).

quiz.q: Why include null markers ('N') when serializing?
options: Without them, different shapes could produce the same string
They mark where each level ends for the decoder
They keep the string length equal to the node count
They let the decoder skip values it has already seen
quiz.why: Preorder plus null markers determines the tree exactly.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n) for both.

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: Why build a trie of the words instead of searching for each word separately?
options: One DFS per cell explores all words at once, pruning dead prefixes
A trie stores the words in less memory than a list
It stops a single word from reusing a grid cell
So the found words come out in sorted order
quiz.why: Searching word by word repeats the same grid exploration for every word. Reusing cells is prevented by marking, not by the trie.

quiz.q: What do the two heaps hold?
options: Max-heap of the lower half, min-heap of the upper half
Min-heap of the lower half, max-heap of the upper half
A max-heap and a min-heap of all values
One heap of even values and one heap of odd values
quiz.why: The median sits at the heap tops: the largest of the lower half and the smallest of the upper half.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Find Median from Data Stream**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is `add_num` O(log n), `find_median` O(1).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Find Median from Data Stream**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What does one adjacent word pair tell you?
options: The first differing characters give one ordering edge
Every position where they differ gives an ordering edge
Their first characters give one ordering edge
Nothing, unless both words have the same length
quiz.why: Characters after the first difference carry no information, and equal first characters say nothing.

problems.title: One Less
problems.desc:
Given a whole number `n`, return the number that comes **just before** it.

For example, the number just before `5` is `4`.
hints: Your function receives a number called `n`. Whatever comes after the word `return` is what the function hands back as its answer.
The number just before another one is that number minus one. Python uses `-` for subtraction.
Write `return` followed by a calculation that uses `n`. Check it on the example: for 5 you should get 4.
problems.solution:
def one_less(n: int) -> int:
    return n - 1

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Return a value:** `return something` sends `something` back as the answer.
**Indentation:** the `return` line sits 4 spaces in from `def`.

problems.title: Double It
problems.desc: Return twice the value of `n`.
hints: "Twice" a number means the number multiplied by 2.
Python's multiplication sign is `*` (not `x` or `×`).
Return the calculation in one line. For 3 you should get 6, and for 0 you should get 0.
problems.solution:
def double(n: int) -> int:
    return n * 2

problems.title: Rectangle Area
problems.desc: Return the area of a rectangle that is `width` wide and `height` tall (width × height).
problems.starter:
def area(width: int, height: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: The area of a rectangle is its width multiplied by its height.
Both values arrive as the function's inputs (its parameters), so you can use their names directly in a calculation.
Return the product of the two parameters using `*`.
problems.solution:
def area(width: int, height: int) -> int:
    return width * height

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Two parameters:** use both names, `width` and `height`, directly.

problems.title: Change Due
problems.desc:
You buy `items` things that each cost `price`, and hand over `paid`. Return the change you get back.

You always pay enough.
problems.starter:
def change_due(price: int, paid: int, items: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: First work out what you spent in total, then take that away from what you paid.
The total cost is the price of one item times how many items you bought.
Python does `*` before `-` (just like in maths), so you can write the whole thing in one expression. Add brackets if it makes it clearer to you.
problems.solution:
def change_due(price: int, paid: int, items: int) -> int:
    return paid - price * items

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Order of operations:** `*` and `/` happen before `+` and `-`, so `paid - price * items` multiplies first.
**Brackets:** `(price * items)` makes the order obvious, if you prefer.
**A variable for a step:** `acc = cost * elems` then `return handed - acc`.

problems.title: Average of Two
problems.desc: Return the average of `a` and `b` as a **float** (a number with a decimal point). For example, the average of `2` and `4` is `3.0`.
problems.starter:
def average(a: int, b: int) -> float:
    pass
hints: The average of two numbers is their total divided by 2.
In Python, `/` always gives a float (a number with a decimal point), which is exactly what's asked for.
Add the numbers first and then divide. Without brackets, Python divides only the second number, because `/` happens before `+`.
problems.solution:
def average(a: int, b: int) -> float:
    return (a + b) / 2

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **True division:** `/` always gives a float: `4 / 2` is `2.0`.
**Brackets first:** `(a + b) / 2`. Without them, only `b` is divided.
**This task checks the type:** returning `3` instead of `3.0` counts as wrong.

problems.title: Share the Sweets
problems.desc: Share `sweets` equally between `kids`, giving each child as many **whole** sweets as possible. Return a list `[each, left_over]`: how many each child gets, and how many are left.
problems.starter:
def share(sweets: int, kids: int) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: Two different questions: how many whole sweets each child gets, and how many are left over.
`//` divides and throws away the remainder (whole-number division). `%` gives just the remainder.
Return a list with both answers inside square brackets, in the order `[each, left_over]`. For 7 sweets and 2 kids that's `[3, 1]`.
problems.solution:
def share(sweets: int, kids: int) -> List[int]:
    return [sweets // kids, sweets % kids]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Return a list of two values:** `return [first, second]`

problems.title: Is It Even?
problems.desc: Return `True` if `n` is even, otherwise `False`.
hints: A number is even when dividing it by 2 leaves nothing over.
`%` gives the remainder after division, and `==` checks whether two values are equal. A comparison is already `True` or `False`.
Return the comparison directly; you don't need an `if`. Remember 0 is even too.
problems.solution:
def is_even(n: int) -> bool:
    return n % 2 == 0

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Remainder:** `n % 2` is `0` for even numbers and `1` for odd ones.
**Compare:** `==` gives `True` or `False`, so you can return a comparison directly.

problems.title: Power Of
problems.desc: Return `base` raised to the power `exp`. `exp` is never negative.
problems.starter:
def power(base: int, exp: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: "Raised to the power" means multiplying the base by itself `exp` times. For example, 2 to the power 3 is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
Python has a power operator: two stars, `**`.
Anything to the power 0 is 1, and the operator already handles that for you.
problems.solution:
def power(base: int, exp: int) -> int:
    return base ** exp

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Power:** `base ** exp`. (`^` is *not* power in Python; it's a bit operation.)

problems.title: Can Vote
problems.desc: People can vote from age 18. Return `True` if someone aged `age` can vote.
hints: You need a yes/no answer, which in Python is `True` or `False`.
A comparison like `x > 5` already produces `True` or `False`, so you can return it directly.
Be careful at exactly 18: someone aged 18 *can* vote, so use "greater than or equal to", which is `>=`.
problems.solution:
def can_vote(age: int) -> bool:
    return age >= 18

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Return the comparison itself:** `return years >= 18` already is `True` or `False`.

problems.title: Different Values
problems.desc: Return `True` if `a` and `b` are different numbers.
problems.starter:
def different(a: int, b: int) -> bool:
    pass
hints: You're asking "are these two numbers different?", and the answer is `True` or `False`.
Python's "not equal" operator is `!=` (an exclamation mark followed by an equals sign).
Return the comparison itself; no `if` is needed.
problems.solution:
def different(a: int, b: int) -> bool:
    return a != b

problems.title: Truthy or Falsy
problems.desc: Return what `bool` says about `n`: `False` for `0`, `True` for any other number.
hints: Python treats every number as "true-ish" or "false-ish" (truthy or falsy): 0 counts as false, and any other number counts as true.
The built-in function `bool(...)` turns a value into exactly `True` or `False` using that rule.
Return the result of calling it on `n`. Negative numbers are truthy too.
problems.solution:
def is_truthy(n: int) -> bool:
    return bool(n)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Convert to True/False:** `bool(n)` is `False` only for zero.

problems.title: Sign of a Number
problems.desc: Return `1` if `n` is positive, `-1` if it's negative, and `0` if it's zero.
hints: There are three cases (positive, negative, zero), and each one returns a different number.
`if` checks the first condition, `elif` ("else if") checks the next one, and `else` catches everything left over.
Check `n > 0` first, then `n < 0`; whatever is left must be zero. Note that 0 is neither positive nor negative.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Colons and indentation:** each condition line ends with `:`, and its block is indented 4 more spaces.
**Return inside a branch:** `return 1` ends the function right there.

problems.title: Letter Grade
problems.desc: Turn a test `score` (0–100) into a letter: 90 and above is `"A"`, 80–89 `"B"`, 70–79 `"C"`, and anything lower `"F"`.
hints: Check the grades from the top down: once a score is 90 or more you know it's an A, and you don't need to check anything else.
Use `if` for the first band and `elif` for the following ones. Each branch returns its letter, which is text in quotes.
Because you check from the top, the B test only needs `score >= 80`: anything 90 or more was already caught by the A test. Mind the edges: exactly 90 is an A, exactly 80 a B.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Several cases:** one `if`, then as many `elif` as you need.
**Order matters:** check `score >= 90` before `score >= 80`, since 95 is also `>= 80`.
**Fallback:** a final `return "F"` (or an `else:`) catches everything else.

problems.title: FizzBuzz (One Number)
problems.desc: Return `"FizzBuzz"` if `n` is divisible by both 3 and 5, `"Fizz"` if only by 3, `"Buzz"` if only by 5, and otherwise `n` as text (for example `"7"`).
hints: "Divisible by 3" means dividing by 3 leaves no remainder, so `n % 3 == 0`.
Order matters. Check "divisible by both" first, because 15 is also divisible by 3 and by 5 on its own. (Divisible by both 3 and 5 is the same as divisible by 15.)
If none of the checks match, return the number as text. `str(...)` turns a number into a string.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Both at once:** `n % 3 == 0 and n % 5 == 0`, or simply `n % 15 == 0`.
**Most specific first:** check FizzBuzz before Fizz and Buzz.

problems.title: In Range
problems.desc: Return `True` if `x` is between `lo` and `hi`, **including** both ends.
problems.starter:
def in_range(x: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> bool:
    pass
hints: "Between `lo` and `hi`, including both ends" means `x` is at least `lo` AND at most `hi`.
You can join two comparisons with `and`. Python also lets you chain them like maths: `a <= b <= c`.
Use `<=` (not `<`) on both sides, so the ends themselves count.
problems.solution:
def in_range(x: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> bool:
    return lo <= x <= hi

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Chained shortcut:** `lo <= x <= hi` means the same thing.

problems.title: Is It the Weekend?
problems.desc: Days are numbered 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday). Return `True` for Saturday (6) or Sunday (7).
hints: The weekend is day 6 or day 7. Any other day isn't.
`or` is `True` when at least one side is `True`.
Compare `day` with each weekend number using `==` and join the two comparisons with `or`. (Writing `day == 6 or 7` is a common mistake: the `7` on its own is always truthy.)
problems.solution:
def is_weekend(day: int) -> bool:
    return day == 6 or day == 7

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Either one:** `or`. Each side needs its own full comparison: `x == 1 or x == 2`, never `x == 1 or 2`.

problems.title: Exactly One
problems.desc: Return `True` if exactly one of `a` and `b` is `True` (not both, not neither).
problems.starter:
def exactly_one(a: bool, b: bool) -> bool:
    pass
hints: There are four combinations of two booleans. You want `True` only for (True, False) and (False, True).
Put another way: at least one is true (`or`), and they're not both true (`not` combined with `and`).
Combine those two ideas with `and`. Use brackets so Python groups them the way you mean.
problems.solution:
def exactly_one(a: bool, b: bool) -> bool:
    return (a or b) and not (a and b)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Group with brackets:** `(p or q)` is worked out before whatever is outside the brackets.
**Shortcut you'll see later:** `a != b` gives the same answer for bools.

problems.title: Add One to Text
problems.desc: You get a number written as text, like `"41"`. Return that number plus one, as an **int** (`42`).
hints: The input is text (a string), and you can't add 1 to text: `"41" + 1` is an error.
`int(...)` turns text made of digits into a whole number.
Convert first, then add one, and return the number (not text).
problems.solution:
def add_one(text: str) -> int:
    return int(text) + 1

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Then add:** `int(text) + 1`. Adding `1` to the text itself is an error.

problems.title: Number to Text
problems.desc: Return the number `n` written as text. For example `12` becomes `"12"`.
hints: You need the same digits, but as text (a string) instead of a number.
`str(...)` turns any value into its text form.
Return the result of calling `str` on `n`. Negative numbers keep their minus sign.
problems.solution:
def to_text(n: int) -> str:
    return str(n)

problems.title: Chop the Decimals
problems.desc: Return `x` with everything after the decimal point removed, as an int. `3.9` becomes `3` and `-2.7` becomes `-2`.
hints: You want to drop everything after the decimal point, without rounding up or down.
`int(...)` on a float does exactly that: it cuts the decimals off (truncation, towards zero).
That's why `-2.7` becomes `-2`, not `-3`. `round` would give a different answer, so don't use it here.
problems.solution:
def chop(x: float) -> int:
    return int(x)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Float to int:** `int(x)` drops the decimals, moving toward zero (so `-2.7` → `-2`).
**Not the same as `//`:** `-2.7 // 1` is `-3.0`, which rounds down instead.

problems.title: Decimal Text Doubled
problems.desc: You get a decimal number as text, like `"2.5"`. Return twice its value as a float (`5.0`).
hints: The input is text that looks like a decimal number, such as `"2.5"`.
`float(...)` turns that text into a decimal number you can do maths with. (`int` would fail, because of the decimal point.)
Convert it first, then multiply by 2, and return the float.
problems.solution:
def doubled(text: str) -> float:
    return float(text) * 2

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Float times int is a float:** `2.5 * 2` is `5.0`.

problems.title: Distance Apart
problems.desc: Return how far apart `a` and `b` are on the number line (always zero or positive).
problems.starter:
def distance(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: The distance between two numbers is their difference, but distance is never negative.
`abs(...)` (absolute value) removes a minus sign: `abs(-4)` is `4`.
Subtract one number from the other and wrap the result in `abs`. Then the order you subtract in doesn't matter.
problems.solution:
def distance(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return abs(a - b)

problems.title: Round the Price
problems.desc: Return `x` rounded to 2 decimal places.
hints: Prices have two decimal places, so round to 2 places.
`round(value, digits)` rounds to that many decimal places. With only one argument it rounds to a whole number, which isn't what you want here.
Pass `x` and the number of decimal places, and return the result.
problems.solution:
def round_price(x: float) -> float:
    return round(x, 2)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Round to places:** `round(x, 2)`. The second argument is the number of decimal places.

problems.title: Largest of Three
problems.desc: Return the largest of the three numbers.
problems.starter:
def largest(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: You need whichever of the three numbers is biggest.
`max(...)` accepts as many numbers as you like, separated by commas, and returns the largest.
One call with all three inputs is enough. Negative numbers work too.
problems.solution:
def largest(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> int:
    return max(a, b, c)

problems.title: Clamp
problems.desc: Return `x`, but forced into the range `lo`…`hi`: if it's below `lo` return `lo`, if it's above `hi` return `hi`.
problems.starter:
def clamp(x: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: Two limits: the answer can't go above `hi`, and it can't go below `lo`.
`min(x, hi)` keeps a number from going above `hi` (it picks the smaller of the two). `max(..., lo)` keeps it from going below `lo`.
Apply one limit, then apply the other to that result, by putting one call inside the other. Test all three cases: below, inside and above the range.
problems.solution:
def clamp(x: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    return max(lo, min(x, hi))

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Nest calls:** `max(lo, min(x, hi))`. The inner call runs first.

problems.title: Say Hello
problems.desc:
Print `Hello, NAME!` using the given `name`. For `"Ada"` that is `Hello, Ada!`.

_This task checks what you **print**, not what you return._
hints: This task checks what you *print* on the screen, not what you return.
`print(...)` shows text. You can join pieces of text with `+`: the greeting, the name, then the exclamation mark.
Watch the exact output: `Hello, ` has a comma and a space after it, and the `!` comes straight after the name with no space.
problems.solution:
def greet(name: str) -> None:
    print("Hello, " + name + "!")

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Join text pieces:** `"Hello, " + name + "!"` (`+` on strings glues them).
**Why not `print("Hello,", name, "!")`?** Commas add spaces, giving `Hello, Ada !`.

problems.title: Two Lines
problems.desc:
Print `a` on one line and `b` on the next line.

_This task checks what you print._
problems.starter:
def two_lines(a: str, b: str) -> None:
    pass
hints: Each `print` call finishes with a new line automatically.
So printing one thing and then printing the other puts them on separate lines.
Use two `print` calls, `a` first and then `b`.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **One `print` per line:** each `print` ends with a new line.

problems.title: Dashed Numbers
problems.desc:
Print the three numbers on one line with dashes between them. For `1, 2, 3` print `1-2-3`.

_This task checks what you print._
problems.starter:
def dashed(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> None:
    pass
hints: When you give `print` several values separated by commas, it puts a space between them by default.
The `sep=` option changes what goes between the values, for example `sep="*"`.
Print all three numbers in one call and set the separator to a dash.
problems.solution:
def dashed(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> None:

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Several values:** `print(a, b, c)` puts spaces between them.

def same_line(a: str, b: str) -> None:

items: **Stay on the same line:** `print(p, end="")`. The next `print` continues right after it.

problems.desc:
Read one line (a name) with `input()`, then print `Hello NAME`.

For the input `Ada`, print `Hello Ada`.

items: **Print two values with a space:** `print("Hello", person)`

problems.title: Add Two Inputs
problems.desc: Read two whole numbers, one per line, and print their sum.

problems.title: String Length
problems.desc: Return how many characters `s` has.
hints: You want the number of characters in the text, counting spaces and punctuation too.
The built-in `len(...)` gives the length of a string (and of lists, and more).
Return what `len` gives you for `s`. An empty string has length 0.
problems.solution:
def length(s: str) -> int:
    return len(s)

problems.title: First and Last
problems.desc: Return the first character of `s` followed by its last character. `"python"` → `"pn"`. `s` has at least one character.
hints: Every character in a string has a position number (an index), starting from 0 for the first character.
Square brackets read one character: `word[0]` is the first. Negative positions count from the end, so `word[-1]` is the last.
Read both characters and join them with `+`. With a one-letter string, the first and last characters are the same letter, so you get it twice.
problems.solution:
def ends(s: str) -> str:
    return s[0] + s[-1]

problems.title: Middle Character
problems.desc: Return the middle character of `s`, which has an odd length. `"abcde"` → `"c"`.
hints: For an odd length like 5, the middle position is 2 (positions 0, 1, **2**, 3, 4).
That middle position is the length divided by 2, using whole-number division `//` so you get an int (indexes must be whole numbers).
Work out the middle index from `len(s)`, then use it inside square brackets.
problems.solution:
def middle(s: str) -> str:
    return s[len(s) // 2]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Middle index:** `len(s) // 2`. Floor division keeps it a whole number.
**Index with an expression:** `word[2 + 1]` works; anything that gives a whole number can go in the brackets.

problems.title: Repeat It
problems.desc: Return `s` repeated `n` times. `"ab"`, `3` → `"ababab"`.
problems.starter:
def repeat(s: str, n: int) -> str:
    pass
hints: Repeating text `n` times is like multiplying it.
In Python, a string times a number repeats it: `"ha" * 2` gives `"haha"`.
Return `s` multiplied by `n`. If `n` is 0 you get an empty string automatically.
problems.solution:
def repeat(s: str, n: int) -> str:
    return s * n

problems.title: First Three
problems.desc: Return the first three characters of `s` (or all of it, if it's shorter).
hints: A slice takes a stretch of a string: `text[start:stop]` goes from `start` up to, but not including, `stop`.
Leave out `start` and the slice begins at the very beginning.
Slices never crash when they go past the end; they just stop at the end. So a short string comes back whole.
problems.solution:
def first_three(s: str) -> str:
    return s[:3]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **From the start up to index 3:** `s[:3]`. It's fine if `s` is shorter.

problems.title: Reverse the Text
problems.desc: Return `s` backwards. `"stressed"` → `"desserts"`.
hints: A slice can have a third number, the step: `text[start:stop:step]`.
A step of `-1` walks backwards through the string.
Leave start and stop empty so the slice covers the whole string, and use a step of -1.
problems.solution:
def reverse(s: str) -> str:
    return s[::-1]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Step of -1:** `s[::-1]` walks the string from the end to the start.

problems.title: Every Other Character
problems.desc: Return the characters at positions 0, 2, 4, …. `"abcdefg"` → `"aceg"`.
hints: You want positions 0, 2, 4, …: start at the beginning and jump 2 each time.
The third slice number is the step size.
Leave start and stop empty (the whole string) and use a step of 2.
problems.solution:
def every_other(s: str) -> str:
    return s[::2]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **A step:** the third number in a slice, `s[::2]`.

problems.title: Drop the Ends
problems.desc: Return `s` without its first and last characters. `"[hello]"` → `"hello"`. If `s` has fewer than 2 characters, return `""`.
hints: You want everything from position 1 up to, but not including, the last character.
`-1` as a slice end means "stop just before the last character".
Slice from 1 to -1. For strings shorter than 2, that slice is already empty, so no `if` is needed.
problems.solution:
def inner(s: str) -> str:
    return s[1:-1]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Stop before the last:** a stop of `-1`.
**Together:** `s[1:-1]`. Slices never raise errors, so short strings just give `""`.

problems.title: Capitalise the First Letter
problems.desc: Return `s` with only its first character changed to upper case. `"hello world"` → `"Hello world"`. `s` may be empty.
hints: Split the job in two: the first character (made upper case) and everything after it (unchanged).
`.upper()` makes text upper case. A slice like `text[:1]` gives the first character, or an empty string if `text` is empty, so it never crashes.
Join the upper-cased first part and the rest with `+`. Using `s[0]` instead would crash on an empty string.
problems.solution:
def cap_first(s: str) -> str:
    return s[:1].upper() + s[1:]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **First character safely:** `s[:1]` is `""` for an empty string, where `s[0]` would crash.
**Rebuild:** strings can't be edited, so build a new one by joining pieces with `+`.

problems.title: Shout
problems.desc: Return `s` in capitals with `"!"` added. `"hey"` → `"HEY!"`.
hints: Two steps: make every letter a capital, then add an exclamation mark.
`.upper()` returns an upper-case copy of the string.
Join the result and `"!"` with `+`.
problems.solution:
def shout(s: str) -> str:
    return s.upper() + "!"

problems.title: Clean Username
problems.desc: Usernames are stored without surrounding spaces, in lower case. `"  Ada_L "` → `"ada_l"`.
hints: Two clean-ups: remove the spaces around the outside, and make everything lower case.
`.strip()` removes whitespace from both ends; `.lower()` makes letters lower case.
You can chain methods: each one returns a new string you can call the next method on.

def clean(s: str) -> str:

items: **Trim whitespace at both ends:** `s.strip()` (spaces, tabs and new lines).

problems.title: Spaces to Underscores
problems.desc: Replace every space in `s` with an underscore. `"my file name"` → `"my_file_name"`.

Call it with a space as `old` and an underscore as `new`, and return the result.

problems.title: Title Case
problems.desc: Capitalise the first letter of every word and lower-case the rest. `"the QUICK fox"` → `"The Quick Fox"`.
hints: Each word should start with a capital, and every other letter should be lower case.
Strings have a built-in method that does exactly this to every word.
Look for the method named after book and film titles. It also fixes words that were ALL CAPS.
problems.solution:
def headline(s: str) -> str:

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Compare:** `s.capitalize()` only capitalises the very first character.

problems.title: Mentions a Cat
problems.desc: Return `True` if the text contains `"cat"` anywhere, in any case. `"My CAT is grey"` → `True`.

`"x" in text` is `True` if the text contains `x` anywhere.

problems.title: Is It a Link?

problems.title: Introduce Someone

hints: You're building a sentence with two values slotted in.

problems.title: Two Decimal Places
problems.desc: Return `x` as text with exactly two decimal places. `3.14159` → `"3.14"`, `2` → `"2.00"`.
hints: You need text with exactly two digits after the point, even for whole numbers (`2` → `"2.00"`).
Inside an f-string's braces you can add a format after a colon. `.2f` means "a float with 2 decimal places".
Put `x` in the braces followed by that format. It rounds for you.
problems.solution:
def money(x: float) -> str:
    return f"{x:.2f}"

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Fixed decimals:** `f"{x:.2f}"`. `.2f` means "a float with 2 decimal places".

problems.title: Zero-Padded Number
problems.desc: Ticket numbers are always 4 digits, padded with zeros. `42` → `"0042"`. Use the built-in `format` function.
hints: The number must always be 4 characters wide, with zeros filling the front.
`format(value, spec)` formats a value using a format spec (the same mini-language as f-strings).
In the spec, `0` means "pad with zeros", `4` is the width and `d` means a whole number. Put those together.

def ticket(n: int) -> str:

items: **Zero-pad to 4 digits:** the spec `"04d"`. Longer numbers aren't cut off.

items: **Percent format:** `.1%` multiplies by 100, shows 1 decimal place and adds `%`.

problems.title: Receipt Line
problems.desc:
Return a 20-character receipt line: the item name left-aligned in 12 characters, then the price right-aligned in 8 characters with 2 decimals.

hints: Two fixed-width columns: the name padded to 12 characters on the left, the price padded to 8 on the right.

problems.desc: Return the letter after `c` in the alphabet, wrapping `"z"` around to `"a"`. `c` is a lower-case letter.

items: **Letter to 0-25:** a letter's code minus the code of `"a"`.

hints: A slice starting `n` places from the end gives the last `n` items.

problems.solution:

problems.title: No Zeros

problems.solution:

Pass that to `all(...)`. Zero isn't positive.

problems.title: Has a Digit

**All of them:** join with `and`. Brackets let one expression span several lines.

problems.title: Every Crate Labelled?
problems.desc:

problems.solution:

problems.title: Harvest Report
problems.desc:
Write the end-of-day report: one line per picker who picked **more than 5** kilos, numbered from 1, biggest picker first.

- **You get:** `names` and `kilos`, the same length.
- **Return:** lines like `"1. Ada (9)"`, ordered by kilos from most to least (equal kilos keep their original order).
- **Example:** `["Bo", "Ada", "Cy"]` and `[6, 9, 2]` → `["1. Ada (9)", "2. Bo (6)"]`.
problems.starter:
def report(names: List[str], kilos: List[int]) -> List[str]:
    pass
hints: Three steps: keep only the big pickers, sort them, then number the lines.
`zip` pairs each name with its kilos; keep the pairs where the kilos are more than 5.
Sort by kilos largest first (sorting is stable, so ties keep their order), then use `enumerate(..., start=1)` to number them.
Build each line with an f-string: number, dot, space, name, then the kilos in brackets.
problems.solution:
def report(names: List[str], kilos: List[int]) -> List[str]:
    pairs = [(k, n) for n, k in zip(names, kilos) if k > 5]
    pairs = sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: -p[0])
    return [f"{i}. {n} ({k})" for i, (k, n) in enumerate(pairs, start=1)]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Turn largest-first into smallest-first:** sort by `-x` instead of `x`.

problems.title: Fence Repair

Work this out for every tree and keep the largest.

def merge(defaults: Dict[str, int], overrides: Dict[str, int]) -> Dict[str, int]:

`.update(other)` copies every key and value from `other` into a dict, replacing any that are already there.

    pass
hints: You want the values the two lists have in common (the intersection).
Convert both lists to sets first.
The `&` operator gives the values that are in both sets.
problems.solution:
def both(a: List[int], b: List[int]) -> Set[int]:
    return set(a) & set(b)

problems.title: The Combined Catalogue
problems.desc:
The two stalls are printing one catalogue together. Every product either of them sells goes in, once.

- **You get:** `a` and `b`, each stall's product numbers.
- **Return:** the set of products in at least one list.
- **Example:** `[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]` → `{1, 2, 3}`.
problems.starter:
def either(a: List[int], b: List[int]) -> Set[int]:
    pass
hints: You want every value that's in one list, the other, or both (the union).
Convert both lists to sets first.
The `|` operator combines two sets.
problems.solution:
def either(a: List[int], b: List[int]) -> Set[int]:
    return set(a) | set(b)

problems.title: Who's Still Missing?
problems.desc:
The market feast is starting. Check the invitations against the people who've arrived.

- **You get:** `invited` and `arrived`, two lists of names.
- **Return:** the invited guests who haven't arrived, in alphabetical order.
- **Example:** `["ada", "bo", "cy"]` and `["bo"]` → `["ada", "cy"]`.
problems.starter:
def missing(invited: List[str], arrived: List[str]) -> List[str]:
    pass
hints: You want the invited guests minus the ones who arrived.
With sets, `-` gives the items in the first set that aren't in the second (the difference).
A set has no order, so pass the result to `sorted(...)` to get an alphabetical list.
problems.solution:
def missing(invited: List[str], arrived: List[str]) -> List[str]:
    return sorted(set(invited) - set(arrived))

problems.title: Swap Meet
problems.desc:
Two traders compare their collections. Anything only *one* of them owns is up for swapping.

- **You get:** `a` and `b`, each trader's item numbers.
- **Return:** the items in one list but not the other, in increasing order.
- **Example:** `[1, 2, 3]` and `[3, 4]` → `[1, 2, 4]`.
problems.starter:
def exactly_one(a: List[int], b: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: You want values in one list or the other, but not in both.
With sets, the `^` operator (symmetric difference) gives exactly that.
Sort the result to get the increasing order the task asks for.
problems.solution:
def exactly_one(a: List[int], b: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    return sorted(set(a) ^ set(b))

problems.title: Can We Bake It?
problems.desc:
The baker has a recipe and a pantry. The recipe can be made if every ingredient it needs is somewhere in the pantry. How much of each doesn't matter.

- **You get:** `needed` (the recipe's ingredients) and `have` (what's in the pantry).
- **Return:** `True` if every needed ingredient is in the pantry, otherwise `False`.
- **Example:** `["egg", "milk"]` and `["milk", "egg", "flour"]` → `True`.
problems.starter:
def can_make(needed: List[str], have: List[str]) -> bool:
    pass
hints: The question is whether everything in `needed` also appears in `have`. Quantities don't matter, which is a clue to use sets.
With sets, `a <= b` is `True` when every item of `a` is also in `b` (a subset).
Convert both lists to sets and compare them. An empty `needed` is always `True`.
problems.solution:
def can_make(needed: List[str], have: List[str]) -> bool:
    return set(needed) <= set(have)

problems.title: Stalls You Missed
problems.desc:
At the end of the day, how many stalls did you never get to?

- **You get:** `stalls` (every stall, possibly listed twice) and `visited` (where you went, with repeats).
- **Return:** how many different stalls you didn't visit.
- **Example:** `["jam", "tea", "bun", "tea"]` and `["tea"]` → `2`.
problems.starter:
def missed(stalls: List[str], visited: List[str]) -> int:
    pass
hints: Repeats don't matter, so sets fit.
With sets, `-` gives the items in the first set that aren't in the second.
Count what's left with `len`.
problems.solution:
def missed(stalls: List[str], visited: List[str]) -> int:
    return len(set(stalls) - set(visited))

problems.title: Bundle a Pair
problems.desc:
Every sale is recorded as an `(item, price)` tuple.

- **You get:** `item` and `price`.
- **Return:** the tuple `(item, price)`.
- **Example:** `"jam", 3` → `("jam", 3)`.
problems.starter:
def bundle(item: str, price: int) -> Tuple[str, int]:
    pass
hints: A tuple is a fixed group of values written with round brackets and commas.
Put the item first and the price second.
Return the tuple.
problems.solution:
def bundle(item: str, price: int) -> Tuple[str, int]:
    return (item, price)

problems.title: Trade Places
problems.desc:
Two stallholders swap pitches for the day.

- **You get:** two numbers, `a` and `b`.
- **Return:** the tuple `(b, a)`.
- **Example:** `1, 2` → `(2, 1)`.
problems.starter:
def swap(a: int, b: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    pass
hints: A tuple is a fixed group of values written with commas, like `(1, 2)`.
You can return several values separated by commas, and Python packs them into a tuple.
Return the two values in swapped order.
problems.solution:
def swap(a: int, b: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    return b, a

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Return a tuple:** `return q, p`. The comma makes the tuple; brackets are optional.
**This task checks the type:** `[b, a]` is a list, so it won't pass.

problems.title: Cheapest and Dearest
problems.desc:
A shopper wants the cheapest and the most expensive price on the board in one go.

- **You get:** `nums`, the prices (at least one).
- **Return:** the tuple `(cheapest, dearest)`.
- **Example:** `[3, 1, 2]` → `(1, 3)`. With a single price, both are that price.
problems.starter:
def low_high(nums: List[int]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    pass
hints: Two answers: the smallest and the largest.
`min(...)` and `max(...)` both work on a whole list.
Return both, separated by a comma, smallest first; that makes a tuple.
problems.solution:
def low_high(nums: List[int]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    return min(nums), max(nums)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Return two results at once:** `return a, b` returns a tuple.

problems.title: First in the Queue
problems.desc:
The market queue: serve the person at the front and keep the rest waiting in order.

- **You get:** `items`, the queue (at least one person).
- **Return:** a tuple `(first person, list of everyone else)`. Use star unpacking.
- **Example:** `[1, 2, 3]` → `(1, [2, 3])`; `[9]` → `(9, [])`.
hints: Unpacking assigns the items of a sequence to several names at once: `a, b = [1, 2]`.
A star in front of a name collects "everything else" into a list: `first, *others = ...`.
Unpack `items` that way, then return the first item and the list of the rest.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Star unpacking:** `leader, *remainder = things`. `remainder` is always a list.

problems.title: As the Crow Flies
problems.desc:
The market map gives each stall as `(x, y)` coordinates. How far is it in a straight line from one stall to another?

- **You get:** `p` and `q`, two `(x, y)` tuples.
- **Return:** the straight-line distance: √((x₁−x₂)² + (y₁−y₂)²).
- **Example:** `(0, 0)` and `(3, 4)` → `5.0`.
problems.starter:
def distance(p: Tuple[int, int], q: Tuple[int, int]) -> float:
    pass
hints: Unpack each point into its x and y: `x1, y1 = p`.
The distance formula: find the difference in x and in y, square both, add them, then take the square root.
Raising to the power `0.5` is a square root (or use `math.sqrt`). Squaring makes negative differences positive.

problems.title: Seal the Order
problems.desc:
Once an order is confirmed it mustn't change, so it's stored as a tuple instead of a list.

- **You get:** `items`, the order as a list.
- **Return:** the same items as a tuple.
- **Example:** `[1, 2]` → `(1, 2)`; `[]` → `()`.
hints: A tuple is like a list that can't be changed.
`tuple(...)` builds a tuple from any sequence.
Return the tuple made from `items`.
problems.solution:
def freeze(items: List[int]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    return tuple(items)

problems.title: Best Sale of the Day
problems.desc:
Each sale is an `(item, price)` tuple. Which item made the single biggest sale?

- **You get:** `sales` (at least one).
- **Return:** the item from the sale with the highest price (the first one if tied).
- **Example:** `[("jam", 3), ("tea", 7), ("bun", 7)]` → `"tea"`.
problems.starter:
def best_sale(sales: List[Tuple[str, int]]) -> str:
    pass
hints: Unpack each tuple straight into two names in the `for` line.
Start with the first sale as the best, unpacked the same way.
Replace the best only when a price is strictly higher, so ties keep the first.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Unpack in a loop:** `for name, cost in pairs:`

problems.title: Map Grid Lookup
problems.desc:
The market surveyor wrote down what stands where as `[x, y, thing]` entries. Turn them into a dict keyed by `(x, y)` tuples, then look up one spot.

- **You get:** `spots` (a list of `[x, y, thing]`) and a position `x`, `y`.
- **Return:** what's at that spot, or `"grass"` if nothing is recorded there.
- **Example:** `[[0, 0, "well"]]` with `0, 0` → `"well"`; with `1, 0` → `"grass"`.
problems.starter:
def at(spots: List[List], x: int, y: int) -> str:
    pass
hints: Tuples can be dict keys because they can't change; lists can't.
Loop over the entries, unpacking each into its two coordinates and the thing, and store the thing under the `(x, y)` tuple.
Look up the asked-for position with `.get`, using `"grass"` as the default.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Unpack three values:** `for a, b, c in rows:`

problems.title: Pitch Map
problems.desc:
Stalls report where they set up as `[x, y]` pairs, and some reported the same spot twice.

- **You get:** `points`, a list of `[x, y]` pairs.
- **Return:** how many different spots there are.
- **Example:** `[[1, 2], [3, 4], [1, 2]]` → `2`.
- **Watch out:** lists can't go in a set, but tuples can.
hints: Lists can't go into a set, because they can change (they're not hashable). Tuples can.
Turn each `[x, y]` into an `(x, y)` tuple with `tuple(...)`.
Put the tuples in a set and count it with `len`.
problems.solution:
def distinct_points(points: List[List[int]]) -> int:
    return len({tuple(p) for p in points})

problems.title: Busiest Spots
problems.desc:
Count how many stalls set up at each spot on the market map.

- **You get:** `points`, a list of `[x, y]` pairs.
- **Return:** a dict mapping each spot, as an `(x, y)` tuple, to how many times it appears.
- **Example:** `[[1, 2], [1, 2], [0, 0]]` → `{(1, 2): 2, (0, 0): 1}`.
hints: This is word counting, but with points as the keys.
Dict keys must be hashable, so turn each point into a tuple first.
Use the counting pattern: get the current count with a default of 0, add one, and store it back.

problems.title: Same Stencils
problems.desc:
Two signs can share a stencil set if they use exactly the same letters (how many times doesn't matter).

- **You get:** two words, `a` and `b`.
- **Return:** `True` if they use the same set of letters. Use `frozenset`.
- **Example:** `"listen"` and `"silent"` → `True`; `"aab"` and `"ab"` → `True`.
problems.starter:
def same_letters(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    pass
hints: Only which letters appear matters, not how many times or in what order.
A `frozenset` is a set that can't be changed. Two of them are equal when they hold the same items.
Make a frozenset from each word and compare them with `==`.
problems.solution:
def same_letters(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    return frozenset(a) == frozenset(b)

problems.title: Stencil Groups
problems.desc:
Group the market's sign words so that words using the same set of letters share one stencil kit.

- **You get:** `words`.
- **Return:** a list of groups, in the order each group's first word appears, with each group's words in their original order.
- **Example:** `["ab", "ba", "aab", "c"]` → `[["ab", "ba", "aab"], ["c"]]`.
hints: Words belong together when they use the same letters, so the set of letters can be the dict key.
A normal set can't be a dict key (it can change), but a `frozenset` can.
For each word, append it to the list stored under its frozenset (`setdefault` makes the list the first time). Return the dict's values as a list.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **A key for "same letters":** `frozenset(w)`. A plain `set` can't be a dict key.

problems.title: Matching Fingerprints
problems.desc:
Dicts and sets find things by their "fingerprint" (their hash). Equal words always get the same fingerprint.

- **You get:** two words, `a` and `b`.
- **Return:** whether their hashes are equal.
- **Example:** `"abc"` and `"abc"` → `True`; `"abc"` and `"abd"` → `False`.
problems.starter:
def same_hash(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    pass
hints: `hash(...)` turns a value into a number that dicts and sets use to find it quickly.
Equal values always have equal hashes.
Compare `hash` of each input with `==`.
problems.solution:
def same_hash(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    return hash(a) == hash(b)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **A value's hash:** `hash(a)`. Equal values → equal hashes; different values almost always differ.

problems.title: Squares You've Walked
problems.desc:
You start at `(0, 0)` on the market grid. Each letter in `steps` moves you one square: `N`, `S`, `E` or `W`. How many **different** squares did you stand on, counting the start?

- **You get:** `steps`, a string of moves.
- **Return:** the number of different squares visited.
- **Example:** `"NESW"` → `4` (you walk a little square and end where you started).
hints: Keep your position as two numbers and a set of every square you've stood on.
Squares go in the set as `(x, y)` tuples (lists can't go in a set).
A small dict from letter to `(dx, dy)` keeps the moves tidy. Start the set with `(0, 0)`, and add each new square after you move.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Add a tuple to a set:** `spots.add((a, b))`

problems.title: The Fast Guest Check
problems.desc:
The guest list is huge, and the door staff check every arrival against it. A list makes each check slow; pick a better structure.

- **You get:** `guest_list` and `arrivals`.
- **Return:** for each arrival, in order, `True` if they're on the guest list.
- **Example:** `["ada", "bo"]` and `["bo", "cy"]` → `[True, False]`.
problems.starter:
def arrived(guest_list: List[str], arrivals: List[str]) -> List[bool]:
    pass
hints: You check membership many times, which is exactly what a set is fast at.
Turn the guest list into a set once, before you start checking.
Then check each arrival with `in` and collect the answers in order.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Is it in the set?** `name in group`
**A list built from a loop:** `[f(x) for x in xs]`

problems.title: Tally in Arrival Order
problems.desc:
Count how many times each item was ordered, and report the items in the order they were **first** ordered.

- **You get:** `orders`, item names in order.
- **Return:** a list of `(item, count)` tuples, in first-order order.
- **Example:** `["tea", "jam", "tea"]` → `[("tea", 2), ("jam", 1)]`.
problems.starter:
def tally(orders: List[str]) -> List[Tuple[str, int]]:
    pass
hints: Counting by name is a dict's job.
Dicts remember the order keys were first added, so the first-order order comes for free.
Count with the read-with-a-default pattern, then turn `.items()` into a list of tuples.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Key and value pairs as a list:** `list(d.items())`

problems.title: Pick the Right Tool
problems.desc:
A quick quiz from the market manager. For each job, name the best structure: `"list"`, `"tuple"`, `"set"` or `"dict"`.

- **You get:** `task`, one of: `"queue"` (customers in arrival order), `"point"` (a fixed `(x, y)` position), `"dedupe"` (remove repeated names), `"phonebook"` (look up a number by name).
- **Return:** the best structure's name.
- **Example:** `"queue"` → `"list"`.
hints: Order and repeats → list. Fixed little bundle → tuple. One of each / fast "seen it?" → set. Look up by a key → dict.
A dict from task name to answer is a tidy way to write the answer table.
Then look the task up in your dict.

problems.title: Loyal Customers
problems.desc:
Each inner list is one market day's customers. A loyal customer came on **every** day.

- **You get:** `days`, at least one day.
- **Return:** the loyal customers in alphabetical order.
- **Example:** `[["ada", "bo"], ["bo", "ada", "cy"], ["bo", "ada"]]` → `["ada", "bo"]`.
hints: Start with everyone from the first day as possible loyal customers.
Each following day, keep only the people who also came that day: that's the intersection, `&`.
Sort what's left at the end.

problems.title: Price Changes
problems.desc:
Compare yesterday's and today's price boards. For every item on **both** boards whose price changed, report `(item, change)` where change = new − old.

- **You get:** `old` and `new`, item → price.
- **Return:** the changes sorted by item name.
- **Example:** `{"jam": 3, "tea": 2}` and `{"jam": 4, "tea": 2, "bun": 1}` → `[("jam", 1)]`.
problems.starter:
def changes(old: Dict[str, int], new: Dict[str, int]) -> List[Tuple[str, int]]:
    pass
hints: Only items on both boards matter. Dict key views support set operations, so `&` finds the shared keys.
Go through the shared items in alphabetical order.
Skip items whose price didn't change; for the rest, record the item with the new price minus the old one.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **The keys of a dict:** `d.keys()` (they work like a set).

problems.title: Busiest Stall
problems.desc:
Each visit is a `(customer, stall)` tuple. The busiest stall had the most **different** customers (a customer who visits twice only counts once).

- **You get:** `visits` (at least one).
- **Return:** the busiest stall; if tied, the one that comes first alphabetically.
- **Example:** `[("ada", "jam"), ("ada", "jam"), ("bo", "tea"), ("cy", "tea")]` → `"tea"`.
problems.starter:
def busiest(visits: List[Tuple[str, str]]) -> str:
    pass
hints: For each stall, keep a **set** of its customers so repeat visits only count once.
A dict from stall to set works well; `setdefault(stall, set())` creates each set the first time.
Pick the stall with the biggest set. To break ties alphabetically, compare `(-size, name)` with `min`.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Get or create a value:** `d.setdefault(k, set())` returns the stored set, creating it the first time.

problems.title: One Candle by Default
problems.desc:
The lighting spell lights candles. Most of the time the wizard wants just one.

- **Write:** `light(candles)`, returning `"lit N"`, where `candles` defaults to `1`.
- **Example:** `light()` → `"lit 1"`; `light(3)` → `"lit 3"`.
hints: A default value goes in the function's first line: `def f(x=5):`.
When the caller leaves the argument out, the default is used.
Build the text with an f-string.
problems.solution:
def light(candles: int = 1) -> str:
    return f"lit {candles}"

problems.title: The Greeting Charm
problems.desc:
The greeting charm says hello to a name. A wizard can change the greeting word, but most never bother, so it should default to `"Hello"`.

- **Write:** `greet(name, greeting)`, returning `"GREETING, NAME!"`.
- **Default:** `greeting` is `"Hello"` when it isn't given.
- **Example:** `greet("Ada")` → `"Hello, Ada!"`; `greet("Ada", greeting="Hi")` → `"Hi, Ada!"`.
hints: A parameter can have a default value that's used when the caller leaves it out.
You write the default in the function's first line (its signature): `def f(a, b="x"):`. Parameters with defaults go after the ones without.
Give `greeting` the default `"Hello"`, then build the result with an f-string: greeting, comma, space, name, exclamation mark.
problems.solution:
def greet(name: str, greeting: str = "Hello") -> str:
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Callers can skip it** (`greet("Ada")`) **or name it** (`greet("Ada", greeting="Hi")`).

problems.title: The Squaring Spell
problems.desc:
The power spell raises a number to a power, but nine times out of ten wizards just want it squared.

- **Write:** `power(x, exp)`, returning `x` raised to `exp`.
- **Default:** `exp` is `2` when it isn't given.
- **Example:** `power(3)` → `9`; `power(3, 3)` → `27`.
hints: The second parameter should be optional, using 2 when it isn't given.
Write the default straight into the signature with `=`.
Return the base raised to the power with `**`. Check both calls: with one argument it squares, with two it uses the given power.
problems.solution:
def power(x: int, exp: int = 2) -> int:
    return x ** exp

problems.title: The Cursed Default
problems.desc:
This tagging spell is cursed. It should start a **fresh** empty list each time it's cast without one, but instead every cast shares the same list. Cast `add_tag("a")` and then `add_tag("b")`, and the second returns `["a", "b"]`.

- **Fix:** `add_tag(tag, tags)` so it appends `tag` to `tags` and returns the list, starting a new empty list whenever no list is given.
- **Example:** casting with `"a"` then `"b"` (no list) gives `["a"]` then `["b"]`.
hints: A default value is created only **once**, when the function is defined, not each time it's called. A default list is therefore shared by every call.
The standard fix: make the default `None`, which never changes.
At the start of the function, if the list is `None`, make a brand-new empty list. Use `is None` for the check, so that an empty list the caller passed in is still used.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Create a fresh list per call:** `if labels is None: labels = []`
**Why:** a default value is evaluated once, when the function is defined, not each time it's called.

problems.title: Format a Scroll
problems.desc:
Format a scroll title between two borders. The options must be given **by name** (keyword-only).

- **Write:** `scroll(title, *, upper=False, border="*")`, returning border + title + border, with the title in capitals when `upper` is true.
- **Example:** `scroll("fire")` → `"*fire*"`; `scroll("fire", upper=True, border="~")` → `"~FIRE~"`.
problems.starter:
def scroll(title: str, *, upper: bool = False, border: str = "*") -> str:
    pass
hints: A bare `*` in the parameter list means everything after it must be passed by name.
Give both options their defaults in the signature.
Choose the title text first (upper-cased or not), then glue the border on both sides.

spec.driver:
def driver(ns, title, upper, border):
    return resolve(ns, "scroll")(title, upper=upper, border=border)

problems.title: How Many Ingredients?
problems.desc:
A potion can take any number of ingredients.

- **Write:** `ingredients(*items)`, returning how many were passed.
- **Example:** `ingredients("newt", "moss")` → `2`; `ingredients()` → `0`.
hints: A star before a parameter collects all the positional arguments into a tuple.
A tuple has a length like any other sequence.
Return its `len`.
problems.solution:
def ingredients(*items: str) -> int:
    return len(items)

spec.driver:
def driver(ns, items):

problems.title: The Gathering Spell
problems.desc:
The gathering spell collects any number of offerings and adds them up.

- **Write:** `add_all`, which accepts any number of numbers (`add_all(1, 2, 3)`) and returns their sum.
- **Example:** `add_all(1, 2, 3)` → `6`; `add_all()` → `0`.
hints: The function must accept any number of values.
A star before a parameter name (`*nums`) collects all the positional arguments into a tuple.
Once you have the tuple, add it up with `sum`. Calling with no arguments gives 0.
problems.solution:
def add_all(*nums: int) -> int:
    return sum(nums)

spec.driver:
def driver(ns, values):
